name: implicit-lock
intent: Make the framework or layer-supertype code that every business operation must pass through acquire and release the locks, so no application method can forget an acquisition and silently invalidate the concurrency policy.
problem: A locking scheme has no gaps only if every path that touches a lockable item acquires its lock: one forgotten acquisition, one lock released too early or too late, makes the whole offline concurrency strategy useless. Because the error shows up only under concurrent conflicting sessions, it survives unit tests, code review and single-user manual testing.
context: Multi-user enterprise applications whose business transactions outlive a single database transaction - a user reads a record, thinks for minutes, then saves - so locks live in a lock table or in version columns rather than in the database transaction. Typically a Unit of Work, a layer supertype, a session facade or a declarative transaction layer already exists, giving the application a place that can own the locking protocol centrally.
benefits: Coverage without discipline: every operation routed through the framework gets the lock, so a forgotten acquisition stops being a possible bug.
Locking policy is centralized: switching from optimistic to pessimistic locking, or widening a lock to its cluster, becomes a change in the framework instead of an edit in every use case.
Business methods contain business logic only - no acquire/release pairs, no hand-written version checks, no lock-order decisions.
The lock set can be derived rather than declared: a Unit of Work already knows which records the transaction read and wrote, so the framework can lock exactly those.
Acquisition, release, timeouts and conflicts are observed in one layer, so the locking scheme becomes measurable; hand-scattered calls cannot be instrumented this way.
Pairs naturally with Coarse-Grained Lock: because the framework decides what to lock, it can widen a single locked record to the cluster that contains it.
tradeoffs: Hidden control flow: whether and which lock is taken is decided by configuration, annotations or interception rather than by the visible code, so reviewing concurrency behaviour requires knowing the framework's interception points.

Policy rigidity: a uniform default forces every operation into the same lock scope; read-only, no-lock or shorter-hold operations need declarative opt-outs that reintroduce the explicitness the pattern removed.

Silent bypass: proxy- or supertype-based acquisition does nothing when the call never passes through the interception point (self-invocation, objects constructed outside the container, data access that skips the session), and the operation then runs unlocked without any error.

Contention amplification: because the framework locks uniformly, an over-broad default (whole aggregate, table or relation) turns rare conflicts into systematic waiting and hides the cost inside 'infrastructure'.

Test blind spot: tests that construct domain objects directly or manage transactions by hand exercise a path production never runs; offline concurrency still needs conflict tests through the real framework path.
Framework coupling: the locking policy becomes a property of the chosen container or ORM, so migrating away means rebuilding it wherever the new framework offers no equivalent hook.

participants.responsibility: The single code path every business operation passes through (transactional proxy, interceptor, session facade or template method); decides which locks a transaction takes and hides the acquire/release calls from application code.
Base class for domain or service classes whose template methods wrap the subclass hook with lock acquisition and release, so a subclass cannot execute a business method outside the locking protocol.
Tracks the objects a business transaction read and modified; this change set is the implicit lock set the framework acquires and releases together with the transaction.

The explicit mechanism underneath - pessimistic lock table, optimistic version column, in-process mutex registry - recording owner and lock type; unchanged by the pattern except that the framework drives it alone.
Carries the version or lock owner and is otherwise unaware of the protocol; business code reads and mutates it normally.
Expresses business logic only; has no lock calls to forget and no lock-order decisions to make, which is the point of the pattern.

use_cases: Request-as-business-transaction: a web application where an ORM Unit of Work or declarative transaction (Spring @Transactional, .NET TransactionScope, Django ATOMIC_REQUESTS) acquires the row locks or version checks for every record the request reads and writes.

Offline edit sessions: a user edits a record for minutes, and the session facade or layer supertype acquires a pessimistic lock when the record enters the business transaction and releases it on commit or abort, so no controller can forget it.
Batch and import jobs that modify aggregates: each chunk runs inside the framework's transactional scope, so locking follows the changed aggregates automatically.

In-process shared state in a service or worker: a scope construct (RAII guard, with block, defer, using declaration, withLock closure) binds release to the lexical block so exceptions and early returns cannot leak the lock.
Multi-tier clients with a session facade: the lock must follow the business transaction rather than the HTTP request, so the facade — not the UI — owns acquisition and release.
Optimistic concurrency: the mapper compares and increments the version column inside the framework's update path, so a hand-written UPDATE statement cannot skip the check.

Microservices saga orchestrator: the orchestrator drives each step inside an implicit transaction scope; each participant's framework layer acquires the lock or version check locally so the saga can compensate without distributed deadlocks.

Event-sourcing projections: a projection handler reads an event stream and writes to a read-model; the handler runs inside an implicit transaction so concurrent projection rebuilds do not corrupt the read-model — the framework decides whether to use optimistic or pessimistic locking based on the change set.

CQRS read-model updates: commands update the write model under an implicit write lock; the read-model update is published as an async event; the projection runs under its own implicit scope with conflict detection (optimistic) rather than blocking (pessimistic).

Database advisory locks for cross-connection coordination: an application holds a PostgreSQL advisory lock across a multi-statement business transaction that is not itself a DB transaction (e.g., involves an external HTTP call in the middle); the lock is acquired via a thin wrapper so callers do not call pg_advisory_lock directly.

Container-managed persistence (EJB CMT, Spring @Transactional): the container acquires and releases locks as part of the transaction lifecycle; developers write business methods without explicit lock calls, relying on the container's implicit concurrency control.

Retry and compensation with implicit lock release: when a business transaction fails after the lock is acquired but before commit, the framework's rollback path releases the lock automatically so the compensating transaction can retry without manual unlock calls.

Spring Framework proxy-managed services: a proxied @Transactional service method is the business entry point; Spring starts or joins the transaction for external calls, so persistence work and its configured optimistic or pessimistic checks stay inside one framework-owned boundary.

Hibernate ORM persistence contexts: an EntityManager or Session transaction can apply @Version optimistic checks or an explicit PESSIMISTIC_WRITE LockMode at the framework boundary, keeping lock acquisition and stale-version detection out of business methods.

EF Core Unit of Work: SaveChanges compares configured concurrency tokens, including SQL Server rowversion, and raises DbUpdateConcurrencyException on a stale update, making the version check implicit in the framework's commit path rather than a hand-written UPDATE predicate.
avoid_when: Single-user, read-only or append-only data where conflicts cannot occur: there is no locking policy to enforce.

One process and one critical section: a plain language scope construct (lock, with, defer, using, an RAII guard) or a single database transaction with row locks is enough - do not build a framework layer for it.

The framework already offers implicit locking (container-managed transactions, ORM sessions with optimistic checks, repository abstractions): configure it instead of building a parallel scheme on top.
Contention is already the dominant cost: a uniform implicit lock makes it worse; change the domain design (shorter transactions, partitioned ownership, optimistic retry) first.

The team cannot operate the framework's transaction semantics (propagation, nesting, rollback rules): implicit locking inherits every subtlety of that machinery, and a locally visible explicit scope may be the more honest choice.
anti_patterns: Explicit lock bookkeeping scattered through business methods (manual lock/unlock pairs, a hand-written SELECT ... FOR UPDATE per query) presented as a locking policy: the first forgotten release or missing acquisition voids it without a failing test.

'Implicit' in name only: annotations or base-class hooks exist, but the code routinely bypasses them (self-invocation, services constructed outside the container, direct SQL that skips the session), so nothing is actually locked.

A global default lock: every read takes an exclusive lock on the whole aggregate, table or relation because the framework cannot distinguish reads from writes, so throughput collapses while the business code looks clean.
Locking at the wrong layer: acquisition coded in the UI controller or in a DAO helper while the Unit of Work keys locks to the business transaction, so lock lifetime and transaction lifetime diverge.
Holding the business transaction — and with it the lock — open across user think time or remote calls, using framework-managed locking to disguise a transaction that is far too long.
Implicit-locking-as-transaction-scope confusion: treating the ORM session flush mode (AUTO vs COMMIT) as an implicit lock strategy when it only controls when SQL is sent, not whether locks are held.
Optimistic-only without a version column: using an ORM's default optimistic behaviour without an explicit @Version or rowversion, so concurrent writes succeed silently instead of raising a conflict.

Self-invocation in Spring without AspectJ: a @Transactional public method calling a @Transactional private method on the same bean runs both inside a single transaction but neither call passes through the proxy, so the outer transaction wraps the inner work with no lock at all.
Assuming container-managed locking means lock-free: EJB @Lock(WRITE) on a singleton still serialises access; treating it as async because the annotation is 'declarative' leads to thread-safety bugs.
design_principles: Make the safe path the default: put the locking protocol behind an interface, template method or interceptor that callers cannot bypass.
Centralize cross-cutting policy: lock acquisition, transaction demarcation and version checking are one responsibility in one layer, not a per-use-case ritual.
Separation of concerns: business logic states what changes, the Unit of Work and framework derive which locks that implies.
Open/closed principle applied to concurrency policy: a new locking strategy extends the framework rather than editing every business method.
Least locking: acquire the narrowest lock the framework can infer and release it when the transaction really ends.
best_practices: Route every business operation through one framework-controlled entry point (service facade, Unit of Work, transactional proxy) and treat bypasses as defects rather than shortcuts.
Let the Unit of Work compute the lock set from the objects actually read and written instead of hard-coding lock calls in use cases.
Provide declarative opt-outs (read-only transactions, no-lock hints, propagation settings) so exceptions are configured rather than hand-coded.
Keep the lock order canonical and configure a lock timeout so contention degrades into a visible exception instead of a hung session.
Instrument acquisition, release, conflict and timeout centrally; a locking scheme that cannot be observed cannot be trusted.
Test through the framework path with two concurrent business transactions that must conflict; hand-managed unit tests exercise a path production does not use.
Bound the lock scope: end the business transaction — and with it the lock — before long think time or remote calls, and use a pessimistic session lock if the work must wait.
Prefer ORM-level optimistic locking (@Version / rowversion) over hand-written version checks; configure the mapper to raise on stale data rather than silently overwrite.

In Spring, avoid self-invocation: a @Transactional method calling another @Transactional method on the same bean bypasses the proxy and runs unlocked; extract to a separate bean or use AspectJ weaving.

In Hibernate, prefer explicit LockMode over relying on implicit session-level locks; use PESSIMISTIC_WRITE for confirmed write intent and PESSIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT when the version must be bumped on lock acquisition.
For .NET TransactionScope, be aware of automatic enlistment and DTC escalation; keep transactions short and avoid crossing process boundaries unless distributed locking is explicitly intended.

Use database-native advisory locks (PostgreSQL pg_advisory_lock, MySQL GET_LOCK) as a framework-of-last-resort when the ORM session is unavailable but the database connection is — this is an explicit lock that can be driven implicitly via a thin wrapper.
Instrument at the connection or session layer so lock timeouts, deadlocks (detected by the DB), and lock wait timeouts surface as concrete exceptions rather than silent transaction rollback.

When using optimistic concurrency, propagate the version conflict to the caller with enough context to retry or present a merge UI; swallowing the StaleObjectStateException leaves the client with no recourse.
